newsitem.title: USA: Hong Kong's Chan vows "no turning back" on liberty.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong's Chan vows "no turning back" on liberty.

text.p: Hong Kong's Chief Secretary Anson Chan has vowed to work for civil liberties and human rights after China takes over on July 1, declaring "you cannot put the clock back" on democratic values.

"I will continue to speak out," Chan, who will continue as Hong Kong's second-highest ranking official after Britain hands the colony back to China, told Newsweek International in an interview published on Sunday.
"The way the civil service works and the way we've been brought up, you're not just there to implement decisions. You're there to give your frank and honest views without bias."
Chan said she supported traditional "Asian values" such as order and obedience, but that these alone would not be enough to run Hong Kong.
"We've been used to freedoms and human rights, and we value these things, too," Chan said in the interview, printed in the magazine's June 6 issue.
"We cannot pretend that Hong Kong is like China. Hong Kong is not like any other province in China. We've progressed at a very different pace. You cannot put the clock back.
"I fully accept that over time what we need to do in Hong Kong is to work out a model of democracy at a pace that the whole community is comfortable with."

Chan, who has served as deputy to British Governor Chris Patten, said she was comfortable with the prospect of working for Tung Chee-hwa, the shipping magnate Beijing has appointed as its first chief executive for Hong Kong.

She added, however, that Tung "doesn't have a real deep understanding of how the government machinery works" and that it would take time for top officials to develop the rapport needed to govern effectively.

Chan, a 35-year veteran official, said she believed it crucial that Hong Kong's civil service remain "politically neutral" and that a legal framework be established for fresh elections in the territory.
She also said she hoped the new government would allow a broad range of political expression in Hong Kong, speaking to fears that Beijing may encourage a clamp-down.

"If the (demonstrations) are legal and they are carried out in a peaceful manner, I certainly would feel it very difficult to support any action that would mean these people would be thrown behind bars," she said.

Chan said she believed Hong Kong was not yet ready for "a full-fledged, Western-style democracy," and that the best way to move forward was by following the Basic Law, the mini-constitution China established for the territory.

The biggest threat to this process, she said, comes not from China's communist leaders but from the people of Hong Kong themselves, some of whom may try to trade freedoms for political clout in Beijing.
